q: Photosynthesis is the chemical reaction that occurs when plants use energy from the sun, carbon dioxide, and water to synthesise the food that the plant needs to survive.
e: True. Photosynthesis is the chemical reaction that occurs when plants use energy from the sun, carbon dioxide, and water to synthesise the food that the plant needs to survive. Oxygen is a product of that reaction, not a starting material.

q: Photosynthesis is the chemical reaction that occurs when plants use energy from the sun, carbon dioxide, and oxygen to synthesise the food that the plant needs to survive.
e: False. Plants use carbon dioxide and water, not oxygen, as the starting materials. Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis.

q: Except for the energy produced from nuclear reactors, all of man's energy resources are chemicals or involve the utilisation of energy through chemical reactions.
e: True. Except for the energy produced from nuclear reactors, all of man's energy resources are chemicals or involve the utilisation of energy through chemical reactions. Fossil fuels, food, and batteries all store or release chemical energy.

q: Except for the energy produced from solar cells, all of man's energy resources are chemicals or involve the utilisation of energy through chemical reactions.
e: False. The exception named in this lesson is nuclear reactors. Solar cells are not that nuclear exception.

q: Whenever a chemical reaction occurs, energy is usually transferred to or from the surroundings.
e: True. Whenever a chemical reaction occurs, energy is usually transferred to or from the surroundings. That transfer is why flasks feel hot or cold.

q: Changing states of matter also involve energy changes.
e: True. Changing states of matter also involve energy changes. Melting and boiling take energy in; freezing and condensing give energy out, with no new substance.

q: Evaporation, melting, condensation, and sublimation are some examples of chemical changes around us in everyday life.
e: False. Those are changes of state, so they are physical changes. No new substance is made.

q: A process that can take place on its own accord is called spontaneous.
e: True. A process that can take place on its own accord is called spontaneous. Spontaneous does not always mean fast; rusting is spontaneous and slow.

q: A process that can take place on its own accord is called non-spontaneous.
e: False. A process that runs on its own is spontaneous. Non-spontaneous changes need a continuous energy push.

q: Non-spontaneous processes need the energy to take place.
e: True. Non-spontaneous processes need the energy to take place. Without a continuous energy supply they do not keep going.

q: Almost all chemical reactions absorb or release energy, generally in the form of heat.
e: True. Almost all chemical reactions absorb or release energy, generally in the form of heat. Chemists track that heat as the enthalpy change.

q: Adding a solution of dilute sulphuric acid to a solution of sodium hydroxide is an example of a spontaneous reaction.
e: True. Adding a solution of dilute sulphuric acid to a solution of sodium hydroxide is an example of a spontaneous reaction. Acid-base neutralisation runs on its own and gives out heat.

q: Adding a solution of dilute sulphuric acid to a solution of sodium hydroxide is an example of a non-spontaneous reaction.
e: False. Acid-base neutralisation of this kind runs on its own, so it is spontaneous. You do not have to keep feeding energy in.

q: The reaction between magnesium and oxygen, and the reaction between copper and oxygen are both non-spontaneous reactions.
e: True. The reaction between magnesium and oxygen, and the reaction between copper and oxygen are both non-spontaneous reactions. Copper needs heating in air; it does not keep reacting on its own at room temperature the way sodium would.

q: Iron rusting is endothermic and spontaneous.
e: False. Rusting is spontaneous, but it is exothermic. The iron-oxygen reaction releases heat overall.

q: When the ice melts at room temperature, that is a spontaneous and endothermic process.
e: True. When the ice melts at room temperature, that is a spontaneous and endothermic process. The ice takes heat from the room, so the process is endothermic even though it happens by itself.

q: When sulphuric acid is slowly poured into water, the flask or beaker becomes hot.
e: True. When sulphuric acid is slowly poured into water, the flask or beaker becomes hot. That heat release means the mixing is exothermic.

q: Exothermic reactions give out energy, so there is a temperature fall.
e: False. If the reaction gives out energy, the surroundings get warmer. A temperature fall would mean heat is being taken in.

q: In exothermic reactions, the energy of the product is lower than the energy of the reactants because energy has been released during the reaction.
e: True. In exothermic reactions, the energy of the product is lower than the energy of the reactants because energy has been released during the reaction. That drop in enthalpy is the definition of an exothermic reaction.

q: When ammonium chloride is dissolved in water, the flask becomes quite cold to the touch.
e: True. When ammonium chloride is dissolved in water, the flask becomes quite cold to the touch. The dissolving takes heat in, so it is endothermic.

q: Endothermic reactions take in energy from the surroundings, so there is a temperature rise.
e: False. Taking heat in cools the surroundings, so the thermometer falls. A temperature rise belongs to an exothermic change.

q: In endothermic reactions, the energy of the products is higher than the energy of the reactants because energy has been absorbed during the reaction.
e: True. In endothermic reactions, the energy of the products is higher than the energy of the reactants because energy has been absorbed during the reaction. That rise in enthalpy is an endothermic reaction.

q: Energy changes in chemical reactions are caused by the making and breaking of chemical bonds.
e: True. Energy changes in chemical reactions are caused by the making and breaking of chemical bonds. Breaking absorbs energy; making releases energy.

q: Energy is released to break bonds, so bond breaking is an exothermic process.
e: False. You must put energy in to break bonds. Bond breaking is endothermic; bond making is the step that releases energy.

q: Energy is released when new bonds form, so bond making is an exothermic process.
e: True. Energy is released when new bonds form, so bond making is an exothermic process. The opposite step, breaking a bond, is endothermic.

q: If the energy absorbed in bond breaking is more than the energy given out in bond making, the reaction is exothermic.
e: False. If bond breaking costs more than bond making returns, the system has absorbed heat overall. That reaction is endothermic.

q: The Law of Conservation of Energy states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed.
e: True. The Law of Conservation of Energy states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed. Energy is never created or destroyed in a chemical change; it only changes form or moves between system and surroundings.

q: Energy can change from one form to another without a net loss or gain of energy and it is called energy transformation.
e: True. Energy can change from one form to another without a net loss or gain of energy and it is called energy transformation. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: The specific part of the universe that contains the reaction or process which is studied is called the surroundings.
e: False. That chosen piece is the system. The surroundings are everything else.

q: Everything in the universe other than the system is called the surroundings.
e: True. Everything in the universe other than the system is called the surroundings. The system is the reaction you are watching; the surroundings are everything else.
